label: Big-O tells you exact runtime
description:
A common shortcut: 'this algorithm is O(n log n), so it runs in n log n operations.' Big-O is an *upper bound* — it tells you what the runtime *can't exceed*, not what it actually is.

**What Big-O actually says**: $f(n) = O(g(n))$ means there exist constants $c, n_0$ such that $f(n) \leq c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \geq n_0$. The actual runtime can be anywhere from very fast to nearly $c \cdot g(n)$.

**Why this matters**:

- **Two algorithms both O(n log n) can differ by 10-100×** in real performance. Mergesort vs Timsort, both $O(n \log n)$, have very different actual runtimes on real data.
- **Constants are often the difference between shipping and not shipping.** Strassen's matrix multiplication is asymptotically faster than the cubic algorithm but has terrible constants — practical only for matrices > ~1000×1000.
- **Cache effects, branch prediction, memory bandwidth dominate for moderate inputs.** A linear-scan O(n) algorithm with good cache behavior can outperform an O(log n) BST on inputs of moderate size.

**Three sibling notations**:

- **Big-O** ($O$): upper bound. 'At most this fast-growing.'
- **Big-Omega** ($\Omega$): lower bound. 'At least this fast-growing.'
- **Big-Theta** ($\Theta$): tight bound. 'Exactly this fast-growing, up to constants.'

When someone says 'mergesort is $O(n \log n)$' they usually mean $\Theta(n \log n)$ (the exact growth rate up to constants). Big-O without quantifier just means 'no slower than'.

**The fix**:

- Treat Big-O as a *first cut* for asymptotic analysis. Always profile actual runtime for real workloads.
- Be precise about Big-O vs Big-Theta when you need to. A '$O(n^2)$ worst case' algorithm might be $\Theta(n)$ on average.
- For production: measure constants, cache behavior, real-world memory layout. Big-O is the start of the analysis, not the end.
probeQuestions: What's the difference between Big-O and Big-Theta?
Two algorithms are both O(n log n). Can one be 100× faster than the other in practice? Why or why not?
Why might an O(n²) algorithm beat an O(n log n) algorithm for moderate input sizes?
correctionPromptTemplate: The learner thinks Big-O = exact runtime. Walk through: Big-O is an upper bound; constants matter; cache + branch prediction often dominate for moderate inputs. Ask: 'two O(n log n) sorts run on the same input. One takes 1 second, the other 10. Is this a contradiction?'
